newsitem.title: UK: Ad execs say alcopop issue about marketing, not ads.
newsitem.headline: Ad execs say alcopop issue about marketing, not ads.

text.p: Advertising executives said on Monday that recent controversy in Britain over so-called "alcopops" had more to do with the way the fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks were packaged -- and not advertised.
The Labour government said on Friday it would study problems caused by alcopops, amid growing concern they helped cause drunkenness and crime among teenagers.
One consumer group, Alcohol Concern, has told the government it wants greater controls on advertising of alcopops, among other things.

But advertising industry officials told Reuters on Monday it was the marketing of alcopops -- that is, packaging and labelling -- that were making the drinks attractive to young people, and that advertising played only a limited role.

They said advertisements placed in various media for alcopops adhered to strict industry codes, but said the fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks were packaged and labelled to make them appeal to young drinkers.
Interior minister Jack Straw said on Friday he asked a team of junior ministers to "consider what further action may be necessary to stop this abuse" of alcopops.

Consumer groups say they are worried alcopops are purposely being marketed to under-age drinkers. The group called Alcohol Concern has been pressing the government for higher taxes and greater controls on advertising and marketing of alcopops, saying it is convinced the drinks are being marketed in a way to make them appealing to young drinkers.

The Portman Group, a watchdog group established by drinks companies, last year upheld complaints alcopops manufacturers were using marketing techniques to target people under the legal age limit of 18. Lionel Stanbrook, deputy director general of Britain's Advertising Association, said the problems have been related to marketing -- including labelling and packaging -- rarther than advertising.
"We make the distinction between the marketing and the advertising," Stanbrook told Reuters. "There are very, very strict rules governing the advertising of alcohol"
Stanbrook, whose trade group represents 27 advertising bodies and professional groups, said alcopops are not a heavily advertised product.
"The difficulty resides in the non-advertising area," he said, notably the packaging and labelling of alcopops.

Alcopops, marketed in brightly labelled bottles under names such as Hooch, Lemonhead and Diamond Zest, and stronger than most beers sold in bars, have become popular in Britain since their launch in 1995. Sales are now worth 265 million pounds a year.
"The key changes are not in the advertising, but in the selling -- packaging and labelling," he said.
Several months before it was elected to government the Labour Party indicated that, if elected, it might tighten rules on advertising alcoholic beverages aimed at young people.

At that time, Nigel Griffiths, Labour's shadow consumer affairs minister, said Labour would not hesitate to introduce statutory regulation if the advertising industry's existing system of self-regulation was not seen to be working.
On May 1 the Labour Party's leader, Tony Blair, was elected in a landslide victory over the Conservative Party's John Major.

Bob Wooton, director of media services for the Incorporated Society of British Advertisers (ISBA), when asked about the alcopops debate, said his group had no problem with government probes in general, but individual industries should not be targeted.
He said ISBA believed there should be freedom to advertise any product that "it is free to sell."
Asked if the Labour Party's move to probe alcopops could be a precursor of how the new government will approach the advertising industry, Wooton said, "It might be."
-- Leslie Adler, London Advertising Newsdesk +44 171 542 2815, leslie.adler@reuters.com
